policy_title: Reform the BBC and scrap the TV licence
stated: Reform UK will reform the BBC, describing it as 'out-of-touch, wasteful, and institutionally biased,' and will scrap the TV licence, arguing that people should be free to choose in a world of on-demand TV.

source.quote: Commence Reform of the BBC The out-of-touch wasteful BBC is institutionally biased. The TV licence is taxation without representation. We will scrap it. In a world of on-demand TV People should be free to choose.

bearing_set.reason: The TV licence (£169.50/year, ~27 million households) is a mandatory household payment; scrapping it would directly reduce a fixed essential bill, producing a real, non-negligible effect on household disposable income.

The policy explicitly claims 'institutional bias' in the UK's primary public broadcaster and frames reform as a free-expression/consumer-freedom issue; changing the BBC's funding model and editorial obligations directly affects the media environment for free expression — a core O9 indicator.
The TV licence carries a criminal sanction for non-payment; scrapping it removes a coercive state mandate, directly improving freedom from state coercion — a core O10 indicator.
The licence fee (£169.50/year) is a flat compulsory household levy; abolishing it increases take-home income for ~26 million paying households, a real and measurable O11 effect.

The licence fee funds ~£3.7bn of BBC expenditure annually; abolition without a specified replacement model creates a material fiscal question — either BBC moves off the public balance sheet (subscription/commercial) or general taxation must fill the gap, both of which move the funded-vs-borrowed indicator.

The flat-rate licence fee is regressive (proportionally heavier on lower-income households); scrapping it reduces a regressive burden, but a shift to subscription access could remove lower-income households' access to public service broadcasting — the distributional direction is genuinely mixed and the gap-widening/narrowing effect is non-negligible.

membership_note: Four fundamentals clear the non-negligible bar: liberty-from-coercion (O10), household tax burden (O11), public finance sustainability given lost earmarked revenue (O12), and distributional incidence of both the removed flat charge and any replacement access model (O14). Effects on services like healthcare or education are too indirect to score without a specified post-reform BBC model.
